---
title: "Build a local development workflow you can keep"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [development]
tags: [local-dev, docker, git, automation]
summary: "You will set up a repeatable local development workflow that keeps your project bootstrapping, commands, and checks in one place."
slug: "local-development-workflow-you-can-keep"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to build a repeatable local development workflow with [Git](https://git-scm.com/), [Docker](https://www.docker.com/), [direnv](https://direnv.net/), and [Just](https://github.com/casey/just) so your project starts the same way every time and new contributors do not have to guess.

## Prerequisites

- Git installed and configured
- Docker and Docker Compose available on your machine
- `direnv` installed and hooked into your shell
- `just` installed for project commands

## Put Environment Rules In The Repository

Your workflow falls apart when setup lives in your memory instead of your repo. Put the defaults where your project can enforce them, but keep secrets out of version control.

Create an `.envrc` file that loads project-local values and keeps shell setup short, because the next step depends on everyone entering the same environment.

```bash
export APP_ENV=local
export APP_PORT=8080
export COMPOSE_FILE=docker-compose.yml
layout bash
```

This gives your project a predictable shell environment whenever you `cd` into the directory. `layout bash` keeps the shell behavior simple, which matters if your commands call other scripts.

Then allow it once:

```bash
direnv allow
```

This tells `direnv` to trust the checked-in `.envrc` for this repo. After that, your environment loads automatically instead of relying on a setup doc you will forget to open.

## Use One Command Surface For Daily Work

A good local workflow answers one question fast: what command do you run next? Put that answer in a `justfile`, because service startup is only useful if the rest of the team runs the same checks.

```make
set shell := ["bash", "-cu"]

start:
	docker compose up -d

stop:
	docker compose down

logs:
	docker compose logs -f app

test:
	docker compose exec app php artisan test

lint:
	docker compose exec app ./vendor/bin/pint --test

reset:
	docker compose down -v
	docker compose up -d --build
```

This gives you one place for the commands you run every day. It also keeps destructive actions like `reset` visible instead of hiding them in ad hoc shell history.

{{< callout type="tip" >}}If a command matters to the project, give it a named recipe. If it is too fragile to name, fix the command before you ask anyone else to run it.{{< /callout >}}

## Keep Services Predictable With Docker Compose

You do not need a complicated container stack for local work. You need stable service names, clear ports, and a startup path that matches the commands you just defined, but that only works if the containers themselves are boring.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    volumes:
      - .:/app
    working_dir: /app
    command: php artisan serve --host=0.0.0.0 --port=8080
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: app
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  postgres_data:
```

This keeps your application and database startup explicit. The named volume preserves database state between runs, while the bind mount lets your code changes appear immediately inside the container.

If you need to explain how these pieces fit together, show the flow instead of narrating it:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[cd into repo] --> B[direnv loads env]
    B --> C[run just start]
    C --> D[docker compose starts services]
    D --> E[run just test or just lint]
```

The workflow stays short on purpose. Enter the repo, load the environment, start services, then run project commands from one command surface.

## Add Bootstrap Steps You Can Rerun Safely

A local setup script should be safe to run twice. That is what makes it useful on day one and after a broken branch switch, but the script still needs to stay readable.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

cp -n .env.example .env || true
just start
docker compose exec app composer install
docker compose exec app php artisan key:generate --force
docker compose exec app php artisan migrate
```

This bootstraps a fresh checkout without assuming much about the machine beyond the tools you listed earlier. The `cp -n` keeps an existing `.env` intact, which makes reruns safer.

## Verify Your Local Development Workflow Works

Do not trust a workflow because it looks tidy. Verify the path a new contributor would actually take, because that is where brittle setup shows up.

{{< steps >}}
{{< step "Open a fresh shell" >}}
Change into the project directory and confirm `direnv` loads your variables without errors.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Start services" >}}
Run `just start` and wait for the containers to become healthy.
{{< /step >}}
{{< step "Run project checks" >}}
Run `just test` and `just lint` to prove the app is usable, not just running.
{{< /step >}}
{{< /steps >}}

You can also add a single verification recipe so the whole check stays easy to remember:

```make
verify:
	just lint
	just test
```

This turns your workflow into something you can run before every commit or after every pull. Once that works, your setup stops being personal knowledge and starts being project infrastructure.

---
title: "Local-first development keeps your feedback loop short"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: ["development"]
tags: ["local-first", "developer-experience", "workflow"]
summary: "Learn what local-first development means, why it matters, and who benefits most from it."
slug: "local-first-development-keeps-your-feedback-loop-short"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

Local-first development means you build and test your work on your machine first, so you can move faster, catch problems earlier, and keep control of your tools and data.

You do not need a staging server for every idea.

You need a setup that answers quickly.

Local-first development is not about hiding from production. It is about shortening the distance between a change and the moment you can trust it.

That shift matters when your work depends on steady repetition. You change a file. You reload. You inspect the result. Then you do it again, but this time with more confidence.

A slow loop trains you to hesitate.

A short loop lets you think with your hands.

If you build apps, scripts, content pipelines, or package code, this approach gives you a cleaner way to work. You spend less time waiting for remote systems to cooperate, but that only helps if your local setup stays honest. The next section is where that tension starts.

## Why local-first development changes how you work

Local-first development gives you speed, but speed is only useful when it stays close to reality. Your machine becomes the place where ideas get tested first, which means your tools, data, and defaults need to match the work you actually ship.

That sounds simple until your local environment drifts from production. Once that happens, fast feedback turns into false confidence. That is the part you need to design carefully.

---
title: "Migrate your frontend toolchain without breaking your build"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: ["development"]
tags: ["vite", "tooling", "migration"]
summary: "You can move to a smaller frontend build setup without losing your current asset flow."
slug: "migrate-your-toolchain-without-breaking-your-build"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to move a project from an older bundler to [Vite](https://vitejs.dev/) so your builds stay predictable while your toolchain gets simpler.

## Prerequisites

- A JavaScript project with an existing build step
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) installed
- One current CSS or JavaScript entry file you can point the new build at

## Replace the Old Build Entry Points

Start by making the new tool responsible for the same files your old build already owns.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build"
  }
}
```

This gives your project a smaller build surface. You keep the same two commands your team already expects, but the work now runs through Vite.

```js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    outDir: 'public/build'
  }
})
```

This sends compiled assets to a stable output directory. That matters during a migration because you want the rest of the app to keep finding files where it expects them.

You have swapped the command layer, but you still need proof that the app is loading the new output.

## Verify the New Toolchain Before You Remove the Old One

Run the new build first. Then check the generated files before you delete anything from the old setup.

```bash
npm run build
ls public/build
```

The first command creates the production assets. The second makes you confirm the output is real before you remove old config files or dependencies.

If your app still points at old bundle names, fix that next. Migration work fails in the handoff, not in the install step.

## Update Your App To Read the New Assets

Your templates, layout files, or backend helpers need to reference the files the new build creates.

```html
<script type="module" src="/build/assets/app.js"></script>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="/build/assets/app.css">
```

This is the simplest possible handoff. It makes the new asset path explicit so you can test it in one place before you abstract it behind helpers.

Once the page renders with the new files, remove the old bundler config and dependencies. Do that last, because a clean migration depends on a working replacement.

---
title: "Write development notes people can use"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [engineering]
tags: [writing, process, documentation]
summary: "Learn how to replace vague development-process language with notes your team can act on."
slug: "write-development-notes-people-can-use"
draft: true
---

Ahnii!

This post shows you how to turn vague development-process notes into clear records that help you and your team decide what to do next.

## Prerequisites

- A place to keep team notes, such as [Markdown](https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/)
- A real change to describe, such as a deploy, migration, refactor, or bug fix

## Replace vague process language with evidence

Words like "momentum," "seamless," "robust," and "transformative" feel useful when you write fast, but they hide the actual state of the work. Your reader still has to ask what changed, what broke, and what needs attention next.

{{< compare >}}
{{< before >}}
The migration gave the team strong momentum. The new setup is seamless, robust, and transformative for day-to-day work.
{{< /before >}}
{{< after >}}
The migration moved 14 jobs from the old worker to the new queue. Three still fail because they expect local disk storage. The next step is updating those jobs to use object storage before the Friday deploy.
{{< /after >}}
{{< /compare >}}

The second version gives your reader something they can verify. It also gives the next section a job: turning that habit into a repeatable writing pattern.

## Use a simple process note template

You do not need a writing framework. You need a short structure that forces specific facts onto the page.

```markdown
## Queue migration - 2026-04-11

What changed: Moved 14 scheduled jobs to the new queue worker.
What works: Email delivery and invoice exports now run on the new worker.
What is broken: Three image jobs still write to local disk.
What is next: Switch those jobs to object storage and redeploy staging.
Who owns it: Platform team.
```

This template keeps you out of summary language and pushes you toward observable state. Each line answers a question your teammate would ask anyway, but the next problem is making the notes useful during review.

## Show the process in the work itself

If your note says a change is stable, show the check that proves it. If your note says a task is blocked, show the command, test, or review state that caused the block.

```bash
php artisan test --filter=ImageJobTest
```

```text
FAIL  Tests\\Feature\\ImageJobTest
- writes processed images to local disk instead of object storage
```

The command tells your reader what you checked. The reformatted output tells them why the work is still open, which sets up the last step: writing notes another person can pick up without a meeting.

## Write handoff notes that survive tomorrow

A good process note should still make sense when you read it the next morning. That means naming the system, the failure, and the next action in plain language.

```markdown
Next action: Update ImageJob to use the storage disk from config, then rerun ImageJobTest before staging deploy.
```

This line gives you one concrete move. It also gives your teammate a clean starting point if the work changes hands.

# Das Boot (1981) — ★★★★

*Directed by Wolfgang Petersen. Starring Jurgen Prochnow, Herbert Gronemeyer, Klaus Wennemann. 149 minutes.*

---

"Das Boot" works because it understands that submarine warfare is mostly waiting, sweating, and listening for the sound that means you are about to die. A lot of war movies use combat as release. This one uses it as pressure. Petersen traps you inside that steel tube with the crew and never lets the air back in, and the result is one of the best films ever made about how war turns men into professionals first and human beings second.

What makes the film great is its discipline. The early patrol scenes are almost routine, but they matter because they show how the crew functions before everything starts to break down. When the U-boat stalks the convoy and the torpedoes finally hit, the sequence is exciting in the usual war-movie sense, but Petersen immediately undercuts that excitement with the sight of burning sailors in the water. The crew has done its job. Nobody celebrates for long. That moral whiplash is the film in miniature. It is never sentimental, but it is never blind to suffering either.

The most famous scenes are still the best ones. The depth-charge attacks are nearly unbearable because the movie understands tactics as well as fear. You always know what is happening: how deep the boat is, what the captain is trying to do, why every creak in the hull matters. There is no chaos for its own sake. The camera squeezes down the corridors, men slam into pipes and bulkheads, gauges shake, sweat drips, and the boat itself starts to feel alive in a bad way, like an animal being beaten to death. A lot of naval films show you the battle. "Das Boot" makes you feel the machinery of it.

Jurgen Prochnow gives the film its center. His captain is competent, cynical, and tired in a way that feels earned rather than theatrical. He is not a cardboard anti-Nazi hero and not a fanatic either. He is a sailor trying to bring his men home while serving a regime the film clearly despises. That balance is one reason the historical authenticity lands so well. "Das Boot" does not clean up the politics of the Kriegsmarine, but it also does not flatten every German sailor into a symbol. It stays with the ugly truth that men can be trapped inside a monstrous war without fully controlling their place in it.

If there is a flaw, it is only that the middle stretch can feel punishingly repetitive on first viewing. Then again, repetition is the point. Patrol, panic, repair, survive, repeat. By the time the film reaches its bitter final turn, that exhaustion has done its work. The ending lands because the movie has earned it.

This is essential viewing for anyone interested in naval warfare, and it holds up on rewatch because the craft is so exact. More than most war films, it also sends you back to the history books, which is always a good sign. "Das Boot" does not glorify war, and it does not reduce it to a sermon. It just shows you the trap, closes the hatch, and waits.

★★★★

---
title: "From Coding Session to Blog Draft Without Losing the Useful Parts"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [ai]
tags: [claude-code, writing-workflow, developer-tools]
summary: "How I turned a technical coding session into a focused blog draft with a clear problem, approach, solution, and takeaway."
slug: "from-coding-session-to-blog-draft"
draft: true
---

## The Problem / Context

A lot of coding sessions feel more useful than the notes they leave behind. You solve a real problem, make a few decisions that matter, maybe back out of one bad approach, and by the end you know something you did not know when you started. Then the session ends and all of that context collapses into a commit message, or worse, disappears entirely.

That was the problem I was trying to solve here: take a coding session and turn it into a blog draft that still reads like a real engineering story. Not a marketing recap, not an AI-generated content blob, and not a changelog pasted into Markdown. I wanted a draft with a clear problem, a believable path through the work, a concrete solution, and a takeaway someone else could actually reuse.

## What I Tried / The Approach

My first instinct was the lazy one: summarize the session chronologically. That usually sounds reasonable until you read it back.

The draft starts turning into this kind of structure:

```text
First I looked at the codebase.
Then I checked the skill instructions.
Then I considered a few options.
Then I drafted the post.
```

That is technically accurate, but it is not a post. It is a log. Readers do not care about every step in sequence. They care about the tension in the work: what was difficult, what was unclear, what changed, and what finally worked.

So I switched to a more deliberate filter.

Instead of asking, "What happened in this session?" I asked four narrower questions:

1. What was the actual problem?
2. What did I try first, including the wrong turn?
3. What solution would another developer want to copy?
4. What did I learn that is still useful after the details fade?

That gave me a much better shape for the post. It also kept the draft from drifting into filler.

I treated the session like source material and extracted only the parts that carried reusable value. In practice that meant dropping incidental details and keeping the engineering arc.

A simple outline helped:

```markdown
## The Problem / Context
## What I Tried / The Approach
## The Solution
## What I Learned
```

That structure is not fancy, but it does something important: it forces the post to earn each section.

If I cannot explain the problem clearly, the draft is not ready.
If the approach section has no trade-off or failed attempt, it probably means I am smoothing over the real work.
If the solution section does not contain something concrete, the post is too abstract.
If the takeaway is vague, then the session probably was not blogworthy in the first place.

I also found that the tone matters as much as the structure. The post works better when I write in first person and admit where the process was messy. Readers learn more from, "I tried the obvious summary first and it flattened the whole session," than from pretending the final structure appeared fully formed.

## The Solution

The solution was to turn the session into a focused Hugo draft with front matter first, then write the body around one strong problem-to-solution arc.

I used a draft structure like this:

```yaml
---
title: "From Coding Session to Blog Draft Without Losing the Useful Parts"
date: 2026-04-11
categories: [ai]
tags: [claude-code, writing-workflow, developer-tools]
summary: "How I turned a technical coding session into a focused blog draft with a clear problem, approach, solution, and takeaway."
slug: "from-coding-session-to-blog-draft"
draft: true
---
```

Then I built the article around the smallest complete story I could tell.

The useful move was not "summarize everything." It was "choose the one lesson with enough depth to stand on its own." In this case, that lesson was that a coding session becomes publishable when you reorganize it around tension and reuse, not around time.

A rough extraction workflow looked like this:

```text
Session transcript or notes
-> identify the core problem
-> keep one failed or incomplete attempt
-> isolate the final working approach
-> write the takeaway in plain language
-> cut everything else
```

That gave me a post that feels like it came from real work instead of being draped over it afterward.

I also kept a few practical rules:

- Lead with the problem, because context creates interest.
- Keep the wrong turn, because it explains why the final approach matters.
- Show concrete structure or code, because abstraction gets slippery fast.
- End with a takeaway, because a post should leave the reader with something portable.

The other important choice was restraint. It is easy to over-explain when turning technical work into prose. I had to keep asking whether a paragraph was carrying insight or just proving that a session happened. If it was the second one, it got cut.

That is the difference between a readable technical post and a polished activity report.

## What I Learned

The biggest lesson is that a good post is not a transcript with better grammar. It is an editorial decision.

A coding session usually contains too much material. Some of it was necessary to get the work done, but not necessary for the reader. The draft improves the moment I stop trying to preserve everything and start shaping the session around what another developer can learn from it.

I also relearned that failed attempts are not waste material. They are often the most valuable part of the story because they explain the boundary of the solution. If I leave them out, the final answer looks simpler than it was, and the post becomes less trustworthy.

If I were doing this again, I would capture candidate blog angles while the session is still fresh instead of waiting until the end. Even one line like "bad first summary flattened the engineering story" is enough to preserve the real insight before it gets cleaned up by memory.

The practical takeaway is simple: when you turn a coding session into a post, do not ask for a summary. Ask for a reusable story. Start with the problem, keep the interesting decision, show the working shape of the solution, and finish with the lesson that survived the session.

That is usually the part worth publishing.

Ahnii!

I spent part of this week in a build session that felt smaller from the outside than it did from inside the work. I was not launching something new. I was trying to make my own foundation hold together better. A lot of my recent time has gone into [Waaseyaa](https://waaseyaa.org), and this session was about getting the framework closer to the kind of tool I can trust when the work gets complicated.

## The Problem / The Why

I keep running into the same tension. I want to move fast enough to keep momentum, but I also need the structure underneath the work to be clear enough that I do not spend half my time remembering what I meant three days ago. That gets harder when I am building across multiple fronts at once.

I have framework work in Waaseyaa. I have product work in [Minoo](https://minoo.live). I have institutional and community-facing ideas tied to [OIATC](https://oiatc.waaseyaa.org). All of it connects back to the same question for me: what does Indigenous digital sovereignty actually look like when it is not just a slogan, but a stack I can run, maintain, and hand to people?

The hard part is not only writing code. The hard part is keeping the code, the specs, the habits, and the direction aligned. When those drift apart, I feel it immediately. A project starts looking active while becoming less coherent. There is motion, but not enough clarity. I have seen enough software go that way to know I do not want to build my own work on top of that kind of fog.

So this build session was about reducing that fog. I wanted tighter links between planning, implementation, and verification. I wanted less ambiguity in the parts of the system that are supposed to protect the rest of the work from entropy.

## What You Built / What You Found

What I built was not flashy. It was the kind of work that usually stays invisible until it is missing.

I spent the session tightening the writing and execution loop around the framework work. That meant making the instructions more usable, making the expected outputs more explicit, and forcing myself to write in a way that leaves less room for vague interpretation later. In practice, that looked like taking loose patterns I had been carrying in my head and turning them into sharper skill and workflow definitions.

That kind of work matters more than it sounds like it should. When I leave too much implied, I end up paying for it later in rework. When the standard is written clearly, I can move with less hesitation. I do not need to renegotiate the same decisions every session.

I also found, again, that a lot of quality problems are really clarity problems. Not brilliance problems. Not effort problems. Clarity. If the voice is muddy, the output drifts. If the structure is muddy, the work bloats. If the workflow is muddy, small tasks turn into long detours.

That showed up even in the writing side of the build. The difference between a personal journal entry and a tutorial is structural, not cosmetic. The difference between grounded voice and generic tech copy is usually whether I am actually saying what happened, plainly, or hiding behind polished language. I do not want polished fog. I want something solid enough to stand on.

There is a broader reason I keep pushing on this. I am trying to build systems that come from my own priorities, my own language, and my own communities, not just systems that imitate whatever the larger industry says matters this quarter. That means the process matters. The discipline matters. The shape of the work matters.

## Where It's Going

The next step is to keep reducing friction between idea, plan, implementation, and release. I want Waaseyaa to feel less like a moving pile of promising parts and more like a framework with a real center of gravity. I want Minoo and OIATC to benefit from that stability instead of constantly depending on improvised structure.

I am not pretending one build session solves that. It does not. But it did move the work in the right direction. It clarified what needs to be stricter, what can stay flexible, and where I am still tolerating too much vagueness.

That is usually how progress actually looks for me. Not a dramatic breakthrough. A better foundation. A cleaner line between what I mean to build and what I am actually building.

Follow the build if you want to watch that take shape. Subscribe, or reply if this kind of slow, real infrastructure work is part of your world too.

## Configure Your Environment

This workflow sets your app configuration before you run it anywhere else.

Start with one local file. Keep secrets out of version control.

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

This creates your working config file from the project template. You edit `.env`, not `.env.example`.

## Set Core Application Values

Open `.env` and fill in the values your app needs first: app name, environment, base URL, and debug mode.

```dotenv
APP_NAME="Inventory Service"
APP_ENV=local
APP_URL=http://localhost:8080
APP_DEBUG=true
```

These values control how the app identifies itself and how it behaves in development. Keep `APP_DEBUG` off outside local work.

## Add Database Credentials

Point the app at the database you want to use. Use local credentials in development, then replace them per environment.

```dotenv
DB_CONNECTION=pgsql
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=5432
DB_DATABASE=inventory
DB_USERNAME=inventory_user
DB_PASSWORD=change-me
```

This tells the app how to open a database connection. If one value is wrong, startup usually fails fast, which is useful here.

## Define External Service Keys

Add API keys after the base app settings work. That keeps early setup simple.

```dotenv
MAIL_API_KEY=your-mail-key
STORAGE_BUCKET=inventory-assets
SENTRY_DSN=https://examplePublicKey@o0.ingest.sentry.io/0
```

These values connect the app to external services. Leave optional integrations blank until you need them.

## Validate the Loaded Configuration

Run the config check before you start the server. It is easier to catch a missing value now than after a failed request.

```bash
php artisan config:check
```

This command verifies required settings and reports missing or invalid entries. Use it any time you change environment values.

## Reload Cached Configuration

If your framework caches config, clear and rebuild that cache after edits.

```bash
php artisan config:clear
php artisan config:cache
```

The first command removes stale values. The second writes a fresh cached snapshot so the app reads the new settings.

## Override Values Per Environment

Keep one baseline example file. Override real values in each deployed environment.

In local development, you usually edit `.env` directly. In staging and production, you usually set the same keys through your host, container platform, or secret manager.

### Keep Environment Names Consistent

Use the same variable names everywhere. Change values, not key names.

That keeps your deploy process boring. Boring configuration is easier to debug.

# Package Overview

This package handles one focused job in your system. You install it when you need that behavior, configure it in code, and keep the rest of your application unchanged.

## Understand What the Package Does

You use this package to add a specific feature without rebuilding the same logic in every project. It gives you a clear entry point, a defined set of options, and predictable output.

The package stays narrow on purpose. You should be able to read the API, understand where it fits, and remove it later without untangling half your codebase.

## See Where It Fits in Your Application

You add the package at the point where your application needs the feature it provides. Your own code still controls when it runs, what data it receives, and how you handle the result.

That keeps the boundary clear. The package does its job. Your application keeps responsibility for business rules and application flow.

## Know What You Get

You get a small surface area to work with. The package exposes the parts you need to configure and hides the internal plumbing you should not have to manage.

You also get a stable way to reuse the same behavior across projects. That reduces copy-paste code and makes changes easier to track.

## Decide When to Use It

Use this package when you need the feature in more than one place or want one maintained implementation instead of several local versions. If the behavior is truly one-off, keeping the code in your application may be simpler.

The right package should save repetition, not add mystery. If you cannot explain why it belongs in your stack after a quick read through the docs, it is probably the wrong dependency.

## Start with the Main Workflow

Read the install instructions first. Then wire the package into the one place in your application where the feature begins.

After that, test the smallest working path. Once that path is clear, you can add configuration, edge-case handling, and any project-specific integration you need.
